json.summary: An elderly woman in an armchair and her bearded grandson (inferred from 'nagyikám') search for a missing butterfly-collecting bag and then reveal an absurd device built around a photo of Tibor, the grandson's father. The woman's deadpan reveals escalate from a 'genius system' that is really a shambles, to a 'helicopter turbine' with a staircase behind it, to preserved body parts (organs in an aquarium, heart in a jam jar), while she keeps swearing 'bazmeg' and praising 'my Tibor'. The humour comes from the bluntly domestic, slang-heavy dialogue clashing with the grotesque and technical content, and from the woman's calm pride as the horror escalates.

characters.name: elderly woman in armchair
characters.description: Old woman with a big puffy bouffant hair and round glasses, seated in a big armchair; she speaks most of the lines, calmly and matter-of-factly, with rough colloquial slang and a strong swearing habit. Her verbal tic is 'bazmeg'/'basszameg' (vulgar 'damn'/'fuck'), used in r6 and r9, and she calls the dead Tibor 'Tiborom' (my Tibor) with pride. She is most likely the bearded man's grandmother ('nagyikám').

characters.name: bearded man
characters.description: Man with a thick full beard and spiky, puffy hair, wearing a short-sleeved shirt and trousers, who stands to the right of the armchair in p0 and p1. He is the grandson and speaks in a mild, anxious register ('Ó jaj...'), addressing the woman as 'nagyikám'. In p2 he is off-panel, but his bubble (r4) trails off to the right toward him.

panels.description: The bearded man stands on the right and the elderly woman sits in the armchair on the left. The bearded man's bubble r0 addresses her ('nagyikám') about the waxed-canvas bag, and her reply r1 'it must be in the sufni!' points to her mouth. His short bubble r2 'Ó jaj...' points to his beard, showing his worry.

The woman holds up a small framed photo of an older bald man with glasses (Tibor, the bearded man's father) while speaking r3, whose tail runs down to her head. The bearded man stands on the right with one hand outstretched in a 'what?' gesture and his bubble tail touches his hair. The background is bare apart from a door frame.

The woman sits in the armchair with a delighted expression. The off-panel bearded man asks r4 'a helicopter turbine?', with his tail running off the right edge of the panel. She answers r5 'yes, the staircase starts right behind it!' with a tail to her mouth. The background has a vertical wall, a door frame, and a railing at the right edge.

The woman is startled, mouth open, in the armchair. Her shout r6 is in a jagged burst reading 'ÁÁÁ!!! BASSZAMEG' with the 'EGY KAUKÁZUSI FÉRFI SZÁRÍTOTT MÚMIÁJA, BAZMEG!!!' text below. Her cloud-shaped bubble r7 'TELEKVITA' has no visible tail and sits beside her head, reading as a thought.

The woman points one finger up in a proud, lecturing pose. Her bubble r9 says the internal organs are soaking in an aquarium, the heart is in a jam jar, and 'FÚJBAZMEG'. Her bubble r10 'TIBOROM PRECÍZ VOLT!' has a tail up to her raised finger, and the small bubble r11 'EMBER' sits next to it. The background is a plain wall with a window frame at right.

notes: 'Nagyikám' is 'nagyi' (granny) plus the informal possessive '-ám', meaning roughly 'my granny', the affectionate form a grandson uses. Keep the form of address (e.g. 'Granny') in r0 so the family relationship is clear.

'Tibor papa' (r0) is colloquial 'Tibor's dad'. The woman later calls Tibor 'Tiborom' (r10, 'my Tibor'), the affectionate possessive she uses for her own son, so Tibor is probably her son and the bearded man's father. Keep the 'my' possessive in r10.

'Lepkegyűjtő felszerelés' is butterfly-collecting equipment, a classic schoolboy/Hungarian hobby. 'Viaszosvászon tarisznya' is a waxed-canvas satchel, an old-fashioned, rural-sounding object that marks the story as a family heirloom. Keep the old-fashioned flavour.

'Sufni' is a small storage nook, cubby, or boxroom, typical of Hungarian family homes. It is the location where the bag must be, so translate it as a generic storage room, not a specific pantry or attic.
'Ó jaj...' (r2) is a mild, resigned 'oh dear/oh no', not a shout. It is the bearded man's only line in the first panel.

p1 r3: 'kibaszott kupleráj' is 'fucking brothel', i.e. a slang term for a chaotic, sleazy, shambolic place. 'Kibaszott' is a vulgar intensifier ('bloody/fucking'). Literal: 'only looks like a fucking brothel'.

p1 r3: 'bomba robbant' literally means 'a bomb explodes'. It is a deliberate double meaning: the device sounds like a bomb went off, which the woman then reframes as a 'genius system'. Keep the explosion image.

p1 r3: 'ráhangolódás' means tuning in or attunement, as with a radio dial or a psychic link. The woman says the photo of Tibor 'helps' the tuning, which is the central absurd premise. Do not over-explain the mechanism; the joke is the deadpan.

p2 r4-r5: the bearded man asks whether the device is a 'helicopter turbine', and the woman says the staircase starts right behind it. This is absurd engineering logic, playing on the idea of a stair-shaped thing behind a machine. Keep the deadpan, matter-of-fact tone.

p3 r6: 'ÁÁÁ!!! BASSZAMEG' / 'BAZMEG!!!' is two spellings of the same vulgar exclamation, 'bazmeg'/'basszameg' (roughly 'fuck/damn'). The spelling variation is deliberate: keep it as-is, and render both as the same swear word, not two different ones.

p3 r6: 'egy kaukázusi férfi szárított múmiája' is 'a dried mummy of a Caucasian man'. 'Kaukázusi' is a dated, classificatory ethnic term, and the wording is deliberately clinical and shocking. Translate with the same flat, anthropological register, and do not soften it into a modern term.

p3 r7: 'TELEKVITA' is not a recognised Hungarian word or name as far as I can tell. It appears in a thought-cloud, so it reads as the woman's private thought. Keep it as drawn (do not translate), and flag it for the team to confirm.
p4 r9: 'Fúj!' is a disgust interjection, roughly 'yuck/ugh'. 'Fújbazmeg' is the woman's swear-disgust combo, the same 'bazmeg' tic as r6.

p4 r9: 'belső szervei itt áznak egy akváriumban' means her internal organs are soaking in an aquarium, and 'a szív külön egy lekváros üvegben' means the heart is separately in a jam jar. 'Lekváros üveg' is a jam jar, a homely household container; the grotesque medical image is deliberately kept in a mundane domestic vessel. Keep the domestic container words.

p4 r10-r11: 'Tiborom precíz volt!' means 'my Tibor was meticulous/precise'. 'Precíz' carries a proud, workmanlike praise, which is the joke: she praises the way the body was preserved. 'Ember!' is a colloquial praise, roughly 'a real man', 'a proper man', said as a verdict on Tibor.

Running gag: the woman's escalating, proud matter-of-fact tone. She keeps lining up a vulgar swear (r6, r9) with a fond or proud statement about Tibor (r10-r11). Keep the swearing and the pride in the same register, and keep 'Tiborom' as a fond possessive every time.

Background signs: there are no readable signs or labels in any panel, so there is no sign-based joke. The only background is a door frame, a window, a wall, and a railing, which should be kept as drawn.

Cultural references: the viaszosvászon bag, the butterfly-collecting hobby, the sufni, and jam jars are all everyday Hungarian household details. The overall gag relies on this ordinary domestic world turning into a mummified/ preserved body and an engineered device, so keep the mundane vocabulary rather than modernising it.
